title: Meditations — On Judgment, Kinship, and Cooperation
author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ἕωθεν προλέγειν ἑαυτῷ· συντεύξομαι περιέργῳ, ἀχαρίστῳ, ὑβριστῇ, δολερῷ, βασκάνῳ, ἀκοινωνήτῳ· πάντα ταῦτα συμβέβηκεν ἐκείνοις παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν. ἐγὼ δὲ τεθεαμένος τὴν φύσιν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ὅτι καλόν, καὶ τοῦ κακοῦ ὅτι αἰσχρόν, καὶ τὴν φύσιν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντος ὅτι μοι συγγενής, οὐχὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ αἵματος ἢ σπέρματος, ἀλλὰ νοῦ καὶ θείας ἀπομοίρας μέτοχος, οὔτε βλαβῆναι ὑπό τινος αὐτῶν δύναμαι· αἰσχρῷ γάρ με οὐδεὶς περιβαλεῖ· οὔτε ὀργίζεσθαι τῷ συγγενεῖ δύναμαι οὔτε ἀπέχθεσθαι αὐτῷ. γεγόναμεν γὰρ πρὸς συνεργίαν, ὡς πόδες, ὡς χεῖρες, ὡς βλέφαρα, ὡς οἱ στοῖχοι τῶν ἄνω καὶ κάτω ὀδόντων. τὸ οὖν ἀντιπράσσειν ἀλλήλοις παρὰ φύσιν· ἀντιπρακτικὸν δὲ τὸ ἀγανακτεῖν καὶ ἀποστρέφεσθαι.
source: Τὰ εἰς ἑαυτόν (Meditations), Book II, section 1. Text based on the editio princeps (Xylander, 1559) as collated in the Loeb Classical Library edition, translated by C.R. Haines, Harvard University Press, 1916
selection_notes: Book II, section 1, the opening meditation of Book II. This is a continuous, self-contained philosophical reflection on how to prepare oneself for the day ahead by anticipating encounters with difficult people. The passage moves through a clear logical sequence: (1) the anticipation of meeting people with various vices, (2) the explanation that their behavior stems from ignorance of good and evil, (3) the recognition that the wrongdoer shares in the same rational nature and divine portion as oneself, (4) the conclusion that one can therefore neither be harmed by them nor hate them, since we are made for cooperation like the parts of a single organism. The organic metaphor of bodily cooperation (feet, hands, eyelids, teeth) provides a vivid and memorable conclusion. The passage is rich in concepts essential for semantic analysis: judgment (of others and of good/evil), control (over one's own reactions), kinship and shared nature, cooperation vs. antagonism, and the relationship between knowledge and moral conduct.
normalization_notes: The Greek text uses standard polytonic orthography as established in modern critical editions (spiritus asper and lenis, iota subscripts, acute/grave/circumflex accents). The text follows the Loeb Classical Library edition (Haines, 1916). No modernization or simplification of the Greek has been performed. The semicolons (·) preserve the editorial punctuation of the Haines edition. This passage is Book II, section 1 in its entirety; the Greek word count is approximately 87 words, which is shorter than the target English word count but reflects the dense, aphoristic nature of Marcus Aurelius's composition. The complete section forms a single meditation and cannot be extended without moving into a new topic in section 2.
